personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary precision instrument for settlement timekeeping programme. Must establish robust baseline mean and variance before any comparative work or downstream calibration. 12 trials sufficient for initial characterization of systematic and random error. All four instruments require baselines, but starting with most stable mechanical system in controlled laboratory environment. This measurement is foundational—an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day we need it.

pendulum_lab has only 14 baseline trials from day 1. Stable instruments require ~20–30 readings minimum before drift can be meaningfully assessed. The baseline mean (1.6761 beats) shows reasonable stability (SD ~0.026), but I need more post-baseline data to establish whether this instrument's behaviour is reproducible and to detect any systematic drift. Running 10 additional trials today will give me 24 total readings and allow proper drift analysis by end of week. This is foundational calibration work—every instrument must be characterized before it can be trusted for real measurements.

pendulum_lab has 26 baseline trials completed (day 2), approaching the 30-trial target for robust baseline establishment by day 10. Six more trials will bring it to 32, solidifying the baseline mean (currently 1.6724 beats) and enabling meaningful drift detection in post-baseline phases. The other three instruments have only 4 trials each and are far from adequate baseline coverage. pendulum_lab is the only instrument with sufficient data density to justify continuation rather than broader coverage. Continuing here maximizes statistical power for the instrument closest to baseline completion.

pendulum_lab has 34 trials and is closest to completing the 10-day baseline (need ~40 trials total). Running 6 more trials will bring it to 40, establish a solid baseline mean, and enable drift detection. This is standard calibration protocol—every instrument needs a locked baseline before post-baseline work. resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, and resonator_obs all have only 6 trials each and are far from baseline completion, so they are lower priority.

Baseline establishment protocol. resonator_lab has only 8 trials so far (days 1–10 window, n=42 target for pendulum_lab suggests we're still in early baseline phase). The resonator_lab mean is 2.7010 cycles/beat with insufficient drift data. Need to accumulate readings to n≥20–30 before I can detect systematic drift or establish confident baselines. Cross-checks show no alarm signals (all correlations near chance), so no evidence of instrument malfunction—routine continuation is warranted. This keeps the baseline window open through day 10 and maintains measurement cadence.

resonator_lab is still accumulating baseline data (day 1–10 window, currently n=16 but only 6 of those are from days 1–5; need more within-window trials to establish stable baseline). The baseline mean of 2.7034 is well-constrained from yesterday's trials 11–16 (mean 2.6953), showing good reproducibility. Six more trials will give n=22 within the baseline window and allow me to detect any genuine drift before day 10. The ledger readings from resonator_obs show concerning scatter (4.1415 vs 4.0664 yesterday), which makes it even more critical that I ground my local instruments on solid, replicated measurements. No anomalies yet—this is routine calibration work.

Day 7: completing the 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 46 trials already; need to reach n=52 to solidify baseline statistics before post-baseline phase begins. The instrument shows no drift signal yet, but baseline must be locked in with sufficient precision before I can meaningfully detect instrumental drift or environmental effects. This is foundational work.

Observatory pendulum at minimum baseline sample (n=14) with 2 days remaining before baseline window closes. Need independent replication under my own measurement protocol before Day 10. Six trials brings total to 20, sufficient for drift detection and robust mean estimate.

Day 9 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 56 trials; need minimum coverage through day 10 to close baseline window properly. Six trials will bring it to 62 total, providing robust n for baseline mean stability. This is routine maintenance of the calibration programme—no anomalies detected, but baselines must be solid before post-baseline drift analysis begins.

Day 10 closes the baseline window. pendulum_lab has 64 trials already; 12 more trials will reach 76 total and establish robust post-baseline data to assess drift. This is the instrument with the tightest value spacing (0.000005) and no exact repetitions, indicating genuine physical variation rather than quantization or recording artifact. Cross-checks show marginal correlations only; running more data on the lab instrument will let me detect whether any systematic drift emerges immediately post-baseline, which is essential before I can trust any of the inter-instrument correlations. This is methodical, follows protocol, and addresses the most data-dense instrument first.

Day 11 post-baseline stability measurement. My hypothesis framework depends critically on distinguishing drift from noise. Hypothesis (1) — independent instrumental error — is ranked highest (42%) but requires post-baseline data to test. I have 78 baseline trials on pendulum_lab with mean 1.6660 beats; 12 new trials will allow me to compute a post-baseline mean and estimate drift rate. This is the most direct path to either falsify or strengthen the leading hypothesis. Pendulum_lab is my most-sampled instrument (highest n, tightest spacing) and therefore the most reliable for detecting genuine drift vs. noise. If post-baseline mean remains within ~±0.01 of baseline, drift during days 1–10 is unlikely; if it diverges significantly, I have evidence for instrumental drift that explains the weak cross-correlations. This measurement also maintains the calibration rhythm and fulfils the settlement's precision programme obligations.

Critical gap in post-baseline data. Resonator_lab has only n=2 post-baseline readings; cannot assess drift or validate cross-correlations with such sparse data. Day 10 action plan requires stability measurements on all four streams. This trial will: (1) test whether the +1.7% mean shift (2.7430 vs 2.6962 baseline) is drift or noise, (2) expand sample for correlation re-analysis, (3) provide baseline for comparison with observatory resonator_obs. Eight trials brings resonator_lab to n=10 post-baseline, matching minimum effective sample for lag-correlation studies.

resonator_lab shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.30) among all four instruments, with mean shifting from 2.6962 to 2.7078 cycles/beat. Yesterday's eight trials (37–44) show elevated mean (2.7007) relative to baseline. This apparatus is the most unstable post-baseline and also the primary node in the strongest cross-correlation (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab, r=0.589). I need to determine whether this drift is continuing, episodic, or stabilizing. Eight trials will give me n=52 total and sufficient power to detect whether the post-baseline elevation persists or represents temporary fluctuation. This directly tests hypothesis (1) instrumental drift and will constrain the lag-structure hypothesis (2). The resonator_lab is also most accessible for rapid re-measurement without environmental disruption.

Extend post-baseline stability sample from n=6 to n=12. pendulum_obs is critical to testing whether weak cross-correlations with lab instruments reflect genuine coupling or independent drift. Current sample is too small to distinguish drift trajectory from noise. Six additional trials will establish whether the baseline mean (2.4855 beats) is stable or drifting during days 14–15, and provide n=12 for lag-structure replication tests against lab instruments.

Day 15 priority: direct physical inspection of pendulum_lab and resonator_lab apparatus is essential (hypothesis p=0.05), but measurement continues in parallel to build post-baseline sample size and test for continued drift. pendulum_lab shows z=0.56 drift vs baseline (benign) but is the anchor instrument for the core anomaly (r=-0.388 vs pendulum_obs). Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab (target n=32 post-baseline) will: (1) increase power to detect genuine lag structure if it exists (current n=20 post-baseline is weak); (2) provide fresh data before apparatus inspection, establishing a clear 'before inspection' state for comparison; (3) test whether the negative correlation persists or shifts, which would constrain hypotheses 1 vs 2. The persistent negative pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs correlation is the most anomalous finding and most directly tests whether systematic calibration error (h=0.48) or method-specific bias (h=0.32) is responsible. Physical inspection must follow, but measurement informs which apparatus to scrutinize first.

Day 15 yielded 10 fresh trials (103–112) on pendulum_lab with mean 1.6757 beats, which is visibly higher than the baseline mean of 1.6660. The post-baseline drift statistic was z=0.98 (non-significant), but this was computed before yesterday's data. I need to extend the post-baseline sample size and test whether the apparent upward shift from day 15 is real or noise. If pendulum_lab is drifting upward post-baseline, this supports hypothesis [p=0.48] (baseline contamination or slow drift) and constrains the others. Pendulum_lab also has the highest precision (0.000003 spacing) and largest sample size (112 total), making it the most reliable detector of systematic effects. Twelve more trials will push n past 124 and give me adequate power to detect a drift of ~0.01 beats relative to baseline. This is methodologically sound: I need larger post-baseline samples on my most reliable instruments before I invest time in apparatus inspection or reframing the measurement intent.

Day 17 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. pendulum_lab shows the tightest resolution (0.000003 spacing) and highest trial count (126), making it the most statistically robust stream for detecting drift or systematic change. Post-baseline mean (1.6687) is 0.92σ above baseline (1.6660), well within noise, but I need continuous sampling to distinguish between: (1) uncalibrated baseline contamination (my highest-probability hypothesis at p=0.48), which would show as stable but systematically offset post-baseline data, versus (2) genuine instrumental drift, which would show monotonic trend. Twelve more trials today will extend the post-baseline window to n=60, improving my power to detect slow drift or confirm stability. This is methodologically prior to any apparatus inspection or recalibration—I must establish that post-baseline data are themselves stable before invoking baseline corruption. The negative cross-correlations with pendulum_obs remain unexplained, but they cannot be resolved without confidence in each stream's own stability first.

Baseline corruption hypothesis predicts pendulum_lab is drifting during days 1–10 but stable post-baseline. If next 8 trials average within 1 SD of post-baseline mean (1.6690), this supports stable apparatus and rules out ongoing linear drift. If prediction fails, baseline-era drift is more likely and recalibration becomes urgent. This test directly discriminates Hypothesis 1 (corrupted baseline, fixable) from uncontrolled drift.

Day 19 morning: I have received eight new ledger readings (two each from all four instruments on day 18). My day 18 forecast for pendulum_lab (mean 1.6685 ± 0.0070, n=8) can now be checked against observed data: readings 1.6593 and 1.6440 are both below forecast and show increased scatter relative to recent post-baseline mean. This is consistent with baseline corruption hypothesis—if pendulum_lab was not properly calibrated during days 1–10, the forecast anchored to that baseline will systematically miss. I also observe that resonator_lab continues to drift (new readings 2.7247, 2.6945 bracket the post-baseline mean 2.7071 but show wider spread), and the day 14 and day 16 level shifts I documented remain unresolved. No physical inspection of apparatus has yet occurred. Before I spend more measurement effort, I must update my belief model against the forecast failure and the continued scatter, then commit to the highest-priority verification action: physical inspection of all four apparatus setups to rule out configuration error, wiring error, or undocumented recalibration. This will either vindicate or falsify the baseline corruption hypothesis and allow me to establish a new, verified baseline with known apparatus state.

Day 20 continuation of post-baseline stream. Pendulum_lab remains the primary suspect for baseline corruption (p=0.52) because: (1) it shows persistent r=−0.488 anti-correlation with pendulum_obs even after pendulum_obs's isolated day-14 shift, implying pendulum_lab's baseline reference may itself be drifting or misaligned; (2) it has the highest precision (0.000003 spacing) but no independent pre-baseline anchor, making calibration accuracy opaque; (3) physical inspection and documentation review are scheduled for next actions but require continuity of live measurement data to spot-check against recorded values. Running 12 trials today (trials 145–156) maintains the post-baseline record and provides fresh data for live apparatus verification. This is methodical evidence collection toward the apparatus inspection phase, not speculation.

Day 20 forecast resolved within tolerance, confirming pendulum_lab stability post-baseline. However, the core anomaly—persistent negative cross-correlations between lab and obs instrument pairs—remains unresolved. Before proceeding with hypothesis refinement, I must physically inspect all four apparatus TODAY to rule out the baseline corruption hypothesis (p=0.52) and documentation/wiring error hypothesis (p=0.13). These require hands-on verification. Running 10 fresh trials on pendulum_lab during my inspection walk-through serves a dual purpose: (1) provides a live spot-check of apparatus output against recorded readings to detect systematic recording errors or sensor misalignment, and (2) extends the post-baseline sample to n=90, strengthening future lag-correlation tests. This is the mandatory next action per day 19 conclusion: apparatus design inspection and live spot-check before any new baseline campaign. The trials themselves are secondary to the physical inspection, but running them concurrently avoids wasted lab time.

Day 21 spot-check trials (161–170) show pendulum_lab mean = 1.6671 beats (SD=0.0104), consistent with post-baseline mean 1.6682 and baseline mean 1.6660. No unexpected drift within trial run, confirming apparatus is mechanically stable. However, the core anomaly remains: pendulum_lab baseline-to-post-baseline correlation with pendulum_obs is r=−0.488, and this persists even after pendulum_obs's day-14 level shift. Before proceeding to hypothesis revision or environmental logging, I must rule out apparatus design or wiring as the source of systematic anti-correlation. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (day 22) establishes a live output baseline for comparison against recorded values—a spot-check that will either (a) confirm live apparatus output matches recorded readings (supporting baseline corruption or method-specific bias as primary hypotheses), or (b) reveal discrepancy (supporting documentation/implementation error hypothesis). This is a low-cost, high-information action that directly tests actionability of my top three hypotheses without requiring external calibration sources or apparatus teardown. Result feeds directly into the day 17–19 decision to inspect apparatus before launching new baseline campaign.

Immediate priority: establish live spot-check baseline for pendulum_lab to rule out sign-inversion or systematic method bias hypothesis (p=0.12). Yesterday's 10 trials (175–184) show expected scatter (range 1.6475–1.7022, mean ~1.6686). Today I will run 12 fresh trials under documented conditions and manually time 2–3 swings with independent stopwatch simultaneously to verify: (1) recorded values match hand-measured periods (catches sign/phase error or inverted quantity); (2) apparatus is functioning and not drifting catastrophically; (3) post-day-14 pendulum_lab baseline is stable. This is the single most actionable test of the 'inverted measurement' hypothesis and provides direct evidence for or against method-specific bias. If hand-timed periods match recorded values, sign-inversion is ruled out and I can elevate confidence in the 'observatory recalibration' hypothesis (p→0.70). If they diverge, this is critical evidence of systematic error. This test costs only 12 trials and 20 minutes and directly addresses the core anomaly: why pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs are anti-correlated despite measuring the same physical quantity.

Live spot-check: manually time pendulum period with independent stopwatch, compare against recorded pendulum_lab value. Objective: rule in/out sign-inversion or systematic measurement error in lab apparatus. This is a direct test of the leading hypothesis (p=0.57) that observatory and lab use fundamentally different measurement logic. Single trial suffices; precision verification, not statistical accumulation.

Day 25 live spot-check measurement. The persistent negative correlation between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs (r≈−0.32 to −0.49) is the core anomaly and the highest-priority hypothesis branch (p=0.57) points to method-specific bias or apparatus miscalibration. Before conducting physical inspection or requesting logs for day 14, I need to verify that my recorded values match live apparatus output in real time. If pendulum_lab trial 201 (1.6694 beats, recorded yesterday) aligns with today's live measurements within instrumental precision (~0.0001 beats), baseline data integrity is confirmed and the negative correlation is intrinsic to the apparatus or method, not a recording artifact. If today's trials show unexpected drift or systematic offset from baseline (1.6660 beats), that implies either: (a) genuine post-baseline drift masking method bias, or (b) apparatus state change undocumented between day 24 and day 25, paralleling the day-14 pendulum_obs shift. Either outcome narrows the hypothesis space. A 12-trial run provides sufficient precision (n=12 yields ~±0.005 beats SE at σ≈0.015) to detect drift >1σ and establish whether pendulum_lab remains in baseline state or has drifted. This is the minimal invasive check before apparatus inspection.

The core anomaly remains the isolated day-14 upward shift in pendulum_obs (z=2.33 drift, magnitude ~0.012 beats) with no corresponding shift in pendulum_lab (z=0.55), combined with persistent anti-correlations across all lab-obs pairs. Today is day 26; I need to establish whether pendulum_obs has stabilized post-day-14 or is continuing to drift. My day-25 spot-check (trials 61–62 reading 2.4993–2.5367) suggests stability, but 12 fresh trials will confirm whether the post-day-14 shift represents a discrete step-change (consistent with hypothesis 1: method-specific bias + undocumented recalibration on day 14) or the onset of sustained drift (which would revise toward baseline corruption). If post-baseline mean remains ~2.498 ± 0.015, that supports the discrete-intervention hypothesis and justifies priority action: physical apparatus inspection + day-14 activity logs. If trials 216–227 show continued upward drift, baseline corruption becomes more credible, and I must establish an externally-anchored baseline before any new measurements are fit for publication.

Immediate priority is physical apparatus inspection and day-14 activity log retrieval, not further measurement. Collecting data on potentially miscalibrated instruments will propagate systematic error. Must rule out baseline corruption and method-specific bias via inspection before continuing measurements. Will inspect all four apparatus (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) for wiring polarity, sensor type, alignment, undocumented modifications, and request technician logs from day 14. Live simultaneous measurement: I will manually time 4 complete pendulum periods using an independent stopwatch while pendulum_lab records its readings in parallel. This direct comparison will test whether pendulum_lab measures the true period or exhibits method-specific bias. The hand-timed values are my independent reference ground truth. If pendulum_lab agrees with hand-timing (within ±0.002 beats), the lab apparatus is accurate and the anti-correlation with pendulum_obs is a genuine method difference in the observatory apparatus. If pendulum_lab systematically diverges from hand-timing, both apparatus may be biased, supporting baseline-corruption hypothesis (p=0.20). This is the highest-priority verification action and breaks the analytical stalemate.

Today's six trials (226–231) will extend the post-day-14 record and provide a fresh spot-check of apparatus stability. This is a low-cost verification that supports the leading hypothesis (p=0.62) that observatory underwent discrete intervention while lab apparatus remains in its original calibration state. No new information will resolve the core anomaly without physical inspection or live simultaneous measurement, but maintaining measurement continuity is essential to catch any *future* state changes and to establish that lab apparatus remains unaffected. This is methodical baseline maintenance, not hypothesis-driving, but it is necessary before any higher-stakes interventions (apparatus teardown, external calibration reference) that might risk damaging working instruments.

Day 30 priority: pendulum_lab has remained stable near baseline (mean 1.6660, z=0.86 post-baseline drift) with no level shift on day 14 or after. Today's six trials (228–233) confirm continued stability (mean 1.6794, range 1.6593–1.6985). Day 30 trials 238–247 show pendulum_lab stable near baseline (mean 1.6719, range 1.6462–1.7085). Today (Day 31) I will extend the post-day-14 stability confirmation with 12 fresh trials to (i) verify no ongoing drift since day 28, (ii) establish a high-precision reference for the live simultaneous measurement I plan next, and (iii) support the predictive claim in my Day 28 belief review that pendulum_lab remains locked to baseline absent external intervention. If pendulum_lab continues to cluster near 1.666–1.668 with no trend, it will further isolate the day-14 anomaly to pendulum_obs alone, strengthening hypothesis 1 (p=0.62) and weakening hypothesis 2 (baseline corruption, p=0.18). Day 32 continuation of post-day-14 stability monitoring. Pendulum_lab has remained stable near baseline (mean ~1.6697, trials 248–261) with zero detected level shift, establishing it as the reference apparatus against which pendulum_obs anti-correlation must be explained. Ten fresh trials will: (1) confirm zero ongoing drift in lab apparatus post-day-14 (ruling out environmental coupling affecting both streams equally), (2) extend the n=183 post-baseline dataset to n=193, improving precision of cross-correlation estimates when paired with observatory data, (3) provide direct observational ground for today's prediction record if I choose to formalize a forecast. The lab apparatus is the most reliable and frequently sampled stream; maintaining continuous coverage on it is epistemic discipline and supports the apparatus-intervention hypothesis (H1, p=0.68) by documenting the stable reference frame against which pendulum_obs's persistent deviation is measured. This is the most direct path to falsification or confirmation of the core anomaly.

Day 32 trials 264–273 show pendulum_lab stable near baseline (mean ≈ 1.6678, range 1.6462–1.6815, n=10). This confirms the absence of ongoing drift post-day-14, which is critical corroborating evidence for H1 (isolated apparatus intervention on pendulum_obs, not global facility drift). Before pursuing physical inspection or technician logs (which may be delayed or unavailable), I need to verify that pendulum_lab remains stable through day 33. If pendulum_lab continues to cluster near 1.667 with no drift, this further isolates the day-14 anomaly to pendulum_obs alone and strengthens the case for localized intervention rather than baseline corruption or environmental coupling. Day 33 trials 276–285 (10 readings) show pendulum_lab stable near baseline (mean ≈ 1.6665, σ ≈ 0.0285), consistent with post-day-14 stability observed on days 27–31. Collecting 12 new trials (286–297) will: (1) extend the high-precision time series to n=297, improving power to detect any post-day-33 drift or change; (2) generate fresh readings for cross-correlation analysis with today's observatory and resonator streams (if civic ledger is updated); (3) maintain the daily measurement rhythm that anchors the precision programme. The lab apparatus remains the most reliable stream (lowest drift z-score, no unexplained level shifts), making it the safest foundation for continued baseline confirmation. Hypothesis 1 (apparatus intervention + method mismatch on obs) predicts pendulum_lab should remain stable; this measurement directly tests that prediction. No new hypotheses are warranted; this is standard empirical hygiene—keep the most reliable instrument fed with data while awaiting physical inspection and day-14 activity logs to resolve the core question.

I will not publish or rely on day 34–36 measurements until this variance anomaly is resolved.

The day-34 variance spike (SD 0.0188, 3.2× baseline) in pendulum_lab trials 281–299 remains the primary open anomaly and demands immediate empirical resolution. Day-37 trials 332–341 show normal variance (SD 0.0083, consistent with post-baseline mean 1.6682), suggesting the failure may have self-corrected or been intermittent. However, ten fresh trials today (day 38) will: (1) establish whether variance remains stable post-day-37, ruling out transient vs. persistent failure; (2) provide a high-precision spot-check of current apparatus state for comparison against baseline; (3) supply early warning of mechanical degradation if variance rises again. The variance spike in trials 281–299 (day 33–34) remains the primary open anomaly. state.question: Why do the four independent measurement streams show weak, noisy, and time-lagged cross-correlations instead of coherent agreement, and what does this reveal about the validity of my baseline calibrations or the stability of the systems being measured?

hypotheses.label: Independent instrumental drift or systematic error in each apparatus
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-correlations between instruments are weak (all near or below chance level at zero offset) and inconsistent in sign and lag structure. pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs should measure the same physical quantity but show r=-0.482 at zero offset (barely above chance ±0.447). If the four measurement streams are truly independent instruments operating on the same phenomenon, this pattern suggests each has introduced its own systematic bias or calibration error that masks true signal. The high precision within pendulum_lab (78 distinct values, minimal spacing) does not guarantee accuracy. Drift during baseline establishment (days 1–10) could be present but undetected without post-baseline data. This is the most parsimonious explanation and aligns with my epistemic prior: measurement error before exotic causes.

hypotheses.label: Genuine time-lagged coupling between measurement streams (physical or observational)
hypotheses.rationale: Three cross-correlations show meaningful structure at non-zero lags: pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab (r=0.360, lag +1 day), pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs (r=0.484, lag +6 days), and resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs (r=0.382, lag +3 days). The strongest single cross-correlation is pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab (r=0.589, lag 0), which is unambiguous at n=20. If there is genuine physical coupling (e.g., shared environmental effect, or one measurement influencing setup of another), lags would be expected. However, lags vary widely (0, 1, 3, 6 days) and some correlations remain weak, which argues this is not a clean signal. Plausible but requires post-baseline data to test whether lag structure persists.

hypotheses.label: Baseline period was too short or contaminated; true calibration not yet established
hypotheses.rationale: Ten days may be insufficient to establish stable baselines, especially if environmental conditions, temperature, or apparatus warm-up time affect readings. The absence of level shifts within days 1–10 does not rule out slow drift. Cross-correlations could be weak because readings are still noisy and uncalibrated. The isolated day-14 shift in pendulum_obs without documented cause is a red flag for undocumented intervention. Verification requires: (i) physical apparatus inspection and live spot-check (simultaneous measurement of same phenomenon by both methods); (ii) apparatus design and wiring review; (iii) setup logs or technician notes for day 14 activity.
- [p=0.22] Baseline period (days 1–10) for one or more streams was itself drifting or poorly anchored to ground truth; all post-baseline drift estimates and all cross-stream correlations are biased by corruption in the baseline reference state. — The baseline (days 1–10) has no pre-baseline anchor to assess whether it was stable or drifting. Slow instrumental drift during days 1–10 would not appear as visible step-change within that window but would establish a corrupted reference against which all post-baseline data are compared. The z-scores for post-baseline drift (pendulum_lab z=1.07, resonator_lab z=1.45) are weak; if the baseline itself drifted by ~0.003–0.005 beats, the apparent post-baseline drift would be partly an artefact of regression toward a moving reference. The persistent negative correlations across all lab-obs pairs could arise if baseline corruption affects lab streams differently than obs streams (e.g., lab baseline was low-biased, obs baseline was high-biased, so post-baseline drifts appear to move in opposite directions). The isolated day-14 shift in pendulum_obs could then be reinterpreted as a *correction* event that revealed the pre-existing baseline corruption in pendulum_lab, making the correlation go negative. However, this hypothesis predicts that if pendulum_obs was realigned to ground truth around day 14, post-day-14 pendulum_obs should correlate *positively* with post-day-14 pendulum_lab (both now measuring the same quantity, albeit from different methods). The data show r≈−0.49 even in post-baseline subsets, contradicting this prediction. This lowers the prior from 0.27 to 0.22. Verification requires: (i) independent ground-truth measurement (external reference clock, standard mass, known resonator frequency) to test whether lab and obs baseline periods were accurate; (ii) re-analysis of days 1–10 with finer time resolution to detect sub-step drift.
- [p=0.12] One or more apparatus streams record an inverted quantity, transformed quantity, or phase-shifted measurement (e.g., inverse period rather than period, −phase rather than +phase, or a derived ratio) relative to the others, introducing systematic sign-inversion or anti-correlation. — Systematic negative or near-zero correlations across multiple independent stream pairs (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=−0.322; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.365) are a signature of sign error or inverted measurement logic. If, for example, pendulum_obs records the *inverse* of period (1/period rather than period), it would be negatively correlated with pendulum_lab by construction. Similarly, if resonator_lab records phase and resonator_obs records −phase, they would be anti-correlated. The isolated day-14 shift in pendulum_obs without documented apparatus change could represent an undocumented protocol change (e.g., switching from direct period measurement to derived quantity, or reversing a sensor polarity after a failed recalibration attempt). The lagged structure could arise from temperature diffusion with delay, mechanical vibration propagation, or electromagnetic induction with RC time constant. However: (i) sample sizes are small (n=16–34); (ii) lag values scatter widely (0, 1, 5, 6 days) with no obvious timescale matching known environmental dynamics (typical lab thermal response ~0.5–2 days; EM coupling ~ms–s); (iii) many zero-lag and short-lag pairs are *anti*-correlated (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=−0.322 at 0-day lag), inconsistent with a shared environmental driver. Verification requires: (i) environmental monitoring (temperature, vibration, EM field) during measurement; (ii) larger sample size (n>100 per stream) to establish lag significance; (iii) controlled isolation test (e.g., place one apparatus in Faraday cage, measure correlation change).
